## Diffusion Equation

*References:* Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, Section 2.3; Strauss,
*Partial Differential Equations*, Chapter 2; Crank, *The Mathematics of
Diffusion*.

The **diffusion equation** describes how a conserved quantity (concentration,
heat, probability) spreads from regions of high to low density. The
constant-coefficient case is the [[heat-equation]], which is treated there in
detail. This note covers the general form with variable diffusivity, drift and
reaction terms, its microscopic origin, and its link to
[[brownian-motion]] and the [[fokker-planck-equation]].

:::{.definition data-title="Diffusion Equation"}

Let $u(t,x)$ be the density of a quantity in $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$. The
**diffusion equation** is
$$
u_t=\nabla\cdot\left(D(x)\nabla u\right),
$$
where $D(x)>0$ is the **diffusion coefficient** (diffusivity). When $D$ is a
constant this is $u_t=D\Delta u$, the heat equation with $k=D$.

:::

The equation is the combination of two ingredients:

1. a **conservation law** $u_t+\nabla\cdot\vec J=0$; and
2. a **constitutive law** $\vec J=-D\nabla u$ (Fick's first law).

## Derivation

### From Conservation of Mass

Let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be any subregion. The mass changes only through
flux across its boundary, so by the divergence theorem
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u~dx=-\int_{\partial\Omega'}\vec J\cdot\vec n~dS
=-\int_{\Omega'}\nabla\cdot\vec J~dx.
$$
Since $\Omega'$ is arbitrary, $u_t+\nabla\cdot\vec J=0$. Fick's law
$\vec J=-D\nabla u$ states that the flux points down the gradient with
strength proportional to its steepness, giving
$u_t=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)$.

### From a Random Walk

Consider a particle on the lattice $h\mathbb{Z}$ which, every $\tau$ units of
time, jumps one step left or right with probability $1/2$. If $p(t,x)$ is the
probability of being at $x$ at time $t$ then
$$
p(t+\tau,x)=\tfrac12p(t,x+h)+\tfrac12p(t,x-h).
$$
Subtracting $p(t,x)$ and Taylor expanding,
$$
\frac{p(t+\tau,x)-p(t,x)}{\tau}=\frac{h^2}{2\tau}\cdot
\frac{p(t,x+h)+p(t,x-h)-2p(t,x)}{h^2}.
$$
Taking $h,\tau\to0$ with $h^2/(2\tau)\to D$ fixed gives $p_t=Dp_{xx}$. The
**diffusive scaling** $h\sim\sqrt\tau$ is what produces a non-trivial limit and
is the discrete version of the scaling of Brownian motion.

> *Note:* The microscopic derivation shows that $D$ has units of
> length$^2$/time, and that diffusion is the macroscopic shadow of independent
> random motion of many particles. The equation is therefore also the law of
> the probability density of a single particle.

## Generalisations

:::{.definition data-title="Advection-Diffusion-Reaction Equation"}

Adding a velocity field $\vec V$ and a source/reaction term $R(u)$,
$$
u_t+\nabla\cdot(\vec Vu)=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)+R(u).
$$

:::

The terms are, in order, the time derivative, **advection** (transport, see
[[transport-equation]]), **diffusion** and **reaction**. Important cases:

- **Pure advection-diffusion** ($R=0$): $u_t+\vec V\cdot\nabla u=D\Delta u$
  for constant $\vec V$ with $\nabla\cdot\vec V=0$.
- **Fisher-KPP equation** ($R=ru(1-u)$): logistic growth plus diffusion,
  producing travelling population fronts with speed $2\sqrt{rD}$.
- **Non-linear diffusion** ($D=D(u)$): e.g. the porous medium equation
  $u_t=\Delta(u^m)$, which has finite speed of propagation.
- **Anisotropic diffusion:** $D$ is a positive definite matrix and the equation
  is $u_t=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)$ with $D=D(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$.

:::{.example data-title="Drift-Diffusion in One Dimension"}

The equation $u_t+vu_x=Du_{xx}$ with constant $v$ is solved from the heat
kernel by moving to the frame $y=x-vt$. Setting $u(t,x)=w(t,x-vt)$ gives
$w_t=Dw_{yy}$, so
$$
u(t,x)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}
e^{-(x-vt-y)^2/4Dt}u_0(y)~dy.
$$
The cloud translates at speed $v$ while spreading like $\sqrt{2Dt}$.

:::

## Link with Stochastic Processes

Let $X_t$ solve the [[stochastic-differential-equations|SDE]]
$dX_t=\mu(X_t)~dt+\sigma(X_t)~dW_t$. Its transition density $p(t,x)$ solves
the **Fokker-Planck (forward Kolmogorov) equation**
$$
p_t=-\nabla\cdot(\mu p)+\frac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_{ij}\left((\sigma\sigma^\top)_{ij}p\right).
$$
With $\mu=0$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{2D}$ this is the diffusion equation, so
$X_t=\sqrt{2D}W_t$ has the density $\mathcal{N}(0,2Dt)$ (the heat kernel). See
[[fokker-planck-equation]] and [[kolmogorov-equations]].

The reverse direction is the **Feynman-Kac formula**, which represents the
solution of $u_t=D\Delta u+c(x)u$ as an expectation over Brownian paths (see
[[feynman-kac-formula]]). The [[black-scholes-pde-bspde|Black-Scholes PDE]] is
a diffusion equation after a change of variables.

:::{.theorem data-title="Mean Square Displacement"}

Let $u$ solve $u_t=D\Delta u$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $u(0,\cdot)=\delta_0$.
Then
$$
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|x|^2u(t,x)~dx=2nDt.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

Let $M(t)=\int|x|^2u~dx$. Differentiating under the integral and integrating
by parts twice (boundary terms vanish by Gaussian decay),
$$
M'(t)=D\int|x|^2\Delta u~dx=D\int\Delta(|x|^2)u~dx=2nD\int u~dx=2nD,
$$
since $\Delta|x|^2=2n$ and the total mass is $1$. With $M(0)=0$ the claim
follows.

:::

> *Note:* The linear growth of the mean square displacement in $t$ is the
> signature of ordinary diffusion and is how $D$ is measured experimentally.
> The Einstein relation $D=k_BT/\gamma$ links $D$ to the temperature $T$ and the
> friction coefficient $\gamma$.

## Properties

:::{.theorem data-title="Properties of the Diffusion Equation"}

Let $u_t=\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)$ with $D\ge D_{\min}>0$ on a bounded domain.

1. **Conservation:** with no-flux boundary conditions
   $\vec J\cdot\vec n=0$, the total mass $\int_\Omega u~dx$ is constant.
2. **Maximum principle:** $\min u_0\le u\le\max u_0$ (with zero source, and
   absent flux through the boundary or Dirichlet data in this range).
3. **Energy decay:** with Dirichlet or no-flux boundaries,
   $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2~dx=-2\int D|\nabla u|^2~dx\le0$.
4. **Irreversibility:** the equation is not invariant under $t\to-t$ and
   backward problems are ill-posed.
5. **Convergence to equilibrium:** with no-flux boundaries $u\to\bar u$, the
   mean of $u_0$, exponentially fast at a rate given by the smallest non-zero
   Neumann eigenvalue of $-\nabla\cdot(D\nabla)$.

:::

:::{.proof}

*(3)* Multiply by $u$ and integrate, using the divergence theorem,
$$
\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\int u\nabla\cdot(D\nabla u)
=\int_{\partial\Omega}uD\partial_\nu u~dS-\int D|\nabla u|^2,
$$
and the boundary term vanishes for either type of boundary condition.

*(5)* Expand $u=\sum_ka_k(t)\varphi_k$ in eigenfunctions of the Neumann
problem. Then $a_k'=-\mu_ka_k$, so $a_k(t)=a_k(0)e^{-\mu_kt}$. The first
eigenvalue is $\mu_0=0$ with $\varphi_0$ constant, which carries the mean, and
all other modes decay at rate at least $\mu_1>0$.

:::

> *Note:* Property 4 is the mathematical expression of the second law of
> thermodynamics. Mode $k$ decays at rate $\mu_k\sim k^2$, so running the
> equation backwards would amplify high frequencies without bound, which is
> why deblurring (the inverse of diffusion) is an ill-posed problem.

## Solutions

### Similarity (Scaling) Solution

The equation $u_t=Du_{xx}$ is invariant under $x\to\lambda x$, $t\to\lambda^2t$.
It therefore admits solutions of the form
$$
u(t,x)=t^{-1/2}\,g\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt t}\right).
$$
Substituting $\xi=x/\sqrt t$ gives the ODE $Dg''+\tfrac12\xi g'+\tfrac12g=0$,
that is $(Dg'+\tfrac12\xi g)'=0$, whose integrable solution is
$g(\xi)=Ce^{-\xi^2/4D}$ and recovers the heat kernel
$$
\Phi(t,x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}e^{-x^2/4Dt}.
$$

### Fourier Transform

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ take the Fourier transform
$\hat u(t,\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi\cdot x}u(t,x)~dx$ so that $\Delta\to-|\xi|^2$.
The equation becomes the ODE $\hat u_t=-D|\xi|^2\hat u$ with solution
$\hat u=e^{-D|\xi|^2t}\hat u_0$. Inverting,
$$
u(t,x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\frac{1}{(4\pi Dt)^{n/2}}e^{-|x-y|^2/4Dt}u_0(y)~dy.
$$
Each Fourier mode decays at its own rate $D|\xi|^2$, which makes the
smoothing property transparent: high-frequency content is damped fastest.

### Bounded Domain

For $u_t=Du_{xx}$ on $(0,L)$ with Neumann (insulated) ends the eigenfunctions
are $\cos(n\pi x/L)$ and
$$
u(t,x)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_ne^{-D(n\pi/L)^2t}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L},
$$
with $a_n=\frac2L\int_0^Lu_0\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}~dx$. As $t\to\infty$
$u\to a_0/2$, the average of $u_0$, which is the equilibrium.

:::{.example data-title="Time to Equilibrate"}

The slowest non-trivial mode decays like $e^{-D\pi^2t/L^2}$, so the
equilibration time scales as $L^2/(D\pi^2)$. Doubling the length of the domain
multiplies the time by four. This is why diffusion is efficient at cell scales
(microseconds over micrometres) but hopelessly slow at macroscopic scales
(years over metres for a typical liquid).

:::

### Numerical Solution

The explicit (forward Euler, central difference) scheme in one dimension is
$$
u_i^{n+1}=u_i^n+r\left(u_{i+1}^n-2u_i^n+u_{i-1}^n\right),\qquad
r=\frac{D\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}.
$$
It is stable only if $r\le\frac12$, which is a severe restriction on the time
step. The implicit (backward Euler) and Crank-Nicolson schemes are
unconditionally stable and require solving a tridiagonal system at each step.
See [[finite-difference-methods]].
